details:
AURA-CREW is a self-monitoring tool for astronauts on long missions. An interactive body avatar shows seven body systems with color-coded status. A daily check-in turns the astronaut's own values into an action plan, trend alerts and what-if scenarios. It is decision support only and does not replace the flight surgeon.

Problem: On long missions, communication delays and distance from Earth make real-time medical support harder. Astronauts need a simple way to understand their own health status and know when to contact the flight surgeon.

Solution: AURA-CREW is a prototype web app built around an interactive body avatar. The astronaut taps a body system (cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, respiratory, nervous and others) to see its status and what to do now. A daily check-in with vital signs (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, SpO2) updates a "Today's action plan" instantly.

Decision support: When values leave the expected range, the app shows a clear alert to contact the flight surgeon. Trend watch compares today with the astronaut's own baseline to catch gradual drift early, and what-if scenarios show how changes affect each system. A 1-minute reaction and working-memory check tracks cognitive performance against the astronaut's own baseline.

Space-specific focus: The design follows NASA Human Research Program hazards: microgravity effects on muscle, bone and cardiovascular health, radiation, and isolation.

Tools: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages. No installation needed; it runs in any browser.

Data note: The demo uses synthetic data. All thresholds are assumptions for the prototype, not clinical values.

Use of SI: The code was developed with AI assistance (Claude Code, Anthropic), and the text was drafted with Claude. The demo video narration is AI-generated (text-to-speech). The author chose the sources and directed all work.

Future work: Connect wearable sensor data and evolve the avatar toward a digital twin of the astronaut.
